query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloys, tailoring the grain boundary morphology to be serrated rather than straight improves toughness by more evenly distributing strain and mitigating intergranular crack initiation. This effect is achieved by controlled cooling during heat treatment, which produces a serrated grain boundary profile that interrupts continuous crack paths and reduces local strain concentration, thereby enhancing toughness via more uniform strain distribution.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy processed by rapid cooling after solution treatment, yielding relatively straight grain boundaries that are prone to intergranular cracking at elevated temperatures.
generation.intervention: Modify the cooling rate during the solution heat treatment (for example, reduce the cooling rate) to create a serrated grain boundary morphology.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing (tensile and creep tests) performed at elevated temperatures (around 650°C), as typically employed in selective laser melted HEAs.
generation.structural_mediator: The serrated grain boundary morphology that interrupts continuous grain boundary paths and redistributes strain.
generation.mechanism: A serrated grain boundary disrupts the concentration of strain localization at the boundaries. By increasing the curvature along grain boundaries, the local stress concentration is reduced, delaying intergranular crack initiation and propagation, thereby enhancing both ductility and toughness during high-temperature deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline HEA with straight grain boundaries, samples with serrated boundaries will exhibit a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and prolonged creep rupture life (with reported factors of ~3.5 and ~400 in prior work), indicating enhanced toughness.
generation.baseline: HEA samples processed with rapid cooling that develop straight grain boundaries and, hence, show lower fracture strains and creep rupture lives at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to be valid in HEA systems where toughness loss is primarily governed by intergranular fracture (due to localized strain at grain boundaries) under high-temperature conditions. It may not apply to alloys where other mechanisms (such as severe elemental segregation or deformation-induced phase transformations) primarily control toughness.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of toughness improvement may vary with the specific alloy composition, processing conditions, and testing environment. Additionally, while prior evidence supports the role of serrated boundaries in reducing strain concentration, the full range of microstructural interactions in different HEAs remains to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high‐entropy alloy samples differing only in the cooling rate after solution treatment. Use rapid cooling to generate straight grain boundaries in one set and a controlled slower cooling process to induce serrated grain boundaries in the second set. Subject both sample sets to tensile and creep testing at elevated temperatures (around 650°C).
measurements: Grain boundary morphology characterization via electron microscopy
Local strain distribution mapping (e.g., via digital image correlation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with serrated grain boundaries do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in fracture strain and creep rupture life relative to the baseline samples with straight grain boundaries, or if strain distribution analysis shows no reduction in localized strain at the boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
